Quick answer: If you have a fever, chills, or signs of significant infection like a persistent cough, call your GP or rheumatology nurse. Also seek advice for severe injection site reactions, sudden weight loss, night sweats, or new neurological symptoms like numbness or visual changes. Prompt reporting of symptoms helps manage potential side effects of biologic therapies.

Overview

What to watch for and when to call the rheumatology helpline.

What the evidence shows

UK guidance from NICE, the British Society for Rheumatology and Versus Arthritis consistently emphasises a combined approach: appropriate medication, regular movement, and supportive lifestyle changes. Recent reviews continue to back this consensus.

What this means for you

  • Talk to your clinician. Personalised advice always beats blanket rules.
  • Track your symptoms. Use a simple diary so you can spot patterns over weeks, not days.
  • Move within comfort. Gentle, regular activity protects joints and mood.
  • Watch the warning signs. New swelling, fever, or rapid loss of function deserve same-week review.

Practical next steps

  1. Read our companion piece for a deeper dive: related guidance.
  2. Bring three questions to your next GP or rheumatology appointment.
  3. Share this article with a family member who supports you day to day.

Editorial standards

This article was prepared by the Living With Arthritis Editorial Team and reviewed by our Clinical Review Board against UK NICE guidance and peer-reviewed sources. We update content at least annually.

What the Evidence Says

Large randomised controlled trials and systematic reviews consistently highlight the effectiveness of biologic therapies in reducing disease activity and improving quality of life for people with inflammatory arthritis. Clinical guidelines from leading UK rheumatology bodies underline the importance of carefully balancing the benefits of these powerful medications against their potential side effects, particularly increased susceptibility to infections.

The evidence also points to the value of shared decision-making between you and your healthcare team. This collaborative approach, supported by detailed patient education, leads to better adherence to treatment and improved long-term outcomes. Regular monitoring for side effects and swift action when they arise are key components of safe and effective biologic treatment, as shown in numerous cohort studies.

Common Mistakes to Avoid

Stopping treatment without consulting your doctor: Can lead to disease flares and joint damage. *Always discuss changes with your rheumatologist. Ignoring minor symptoms: Small issues can sometimes escalate into bigger problems. *Report any new or worsening symptoms promptly. Skipping regular monitoring appointments: Crucial for detecting side effects early. *Attend all scheduled blood tests and clinic reviews. Not carrying your patient alert card: Essential for emergency care providers. *Keep your alert card with you at all times. Downplaying infection symptoms: Infections can be more serious on biologics. *Seek medical advice for even minor signs of infection.

When to Speak to a Clinician

It's vital to know when a symptom or situation requires professional medical attention. Don't hesitate to contact your GP, rheumatology nurse, or consultant if you experience any of the following:

  • Fever or chills: Especially if accompanied by new or worsening stiffness, pain, or general unwellness.
  • Signs of significant infection: Such as a persistent cough, shortness of breath, painful urination, or skin redness spreading from a cut or wound.
  • Severe or spreading injection site reactions: Beyond mild redness or tenderness that doesn't resolve within a day or two.
  • Sudden, unexplained weight loss or night sweats: These can be important warning signs that need investigation.
  • New or worsening neurological symptoms: Like numbness, tingling, weakness, or changes in vision.

Frequently Asked Questions

Can I get vaccines while on biologic therapy?

Generally, yes, but it depends on the type of vaccine. Live vaccines, such as for measles, mumps, and rubella (MMR), are usually not recommended. Inactivated vaccines, like the flu jab and pneumonia vaccine, are generally safe and often advised. Always discuss your vaccination schedule with your rheumatology team.

What should I do if I think I'm getting a cold or flu?

If you develop symptoms of a cold or flu, contact your rheumatology team for advice. They may suggest pausing your biologic therapy temporarily until you recover. It's important not to self-adjust your medication without guidance, as pausing can vary depending on the specific biologic and your individual situation.

How do I manage injection site reactions?

Mild reactions like redness, itching, or a small bruise at the injection site are common and usually resolve on their own. Applying a cool compress before and after the injection, ensuring the medication is at room temperature, and rotating injection sites can help. If reactions are severe, painful, or spreading, contact your healthcare provider.

Practical next steps for Biologic Side Effects: Infections, Injections and Monitoring

If you came here about Biologic Side Effects: Infections, Injections and Monitoring, pick one change you can keep for a fortnight rather than overhauling everything at once. Note what hurts, what helps, and what you have already tried, then take that list to your GP, rheumatology nurse or physiotherapist so the conversation stays concrete.

In many areas you can ask your primary care network about self-referral to physiotherapy or lifestyle support without waiting for a hospital letter. Check your GP surgery website or the NHS App for the route that applies where you live.

Preparing for appointments

Write three priorities before you go: main symptom, functional limit (stairs, sleep, work), and the question you most need answered. Bring a current medicine list including over-the-counter products. If English is not your first language, request an interpreter when you book.

Working with NHS pathways

Most people start with GP care, community physiotherapy and self-management, with rheumatology involved when inflammatory disease is suspected or treatment needs escalate. Ask what monitoring blood tests or reviews you should expect, and who to contact between appointments if a flare escalates.

Quick questions about Biologic Side Effects Infections

Is this a substitute for seeing a clinician? No. Use it to prepare questions and understand options, then confirm decisions with your NHS team.

How long before I judge whether a change helped? Give most habit or exercise changes at least two to four weeks, unless pain or swelling clearly worsens — in that case scale back sooner.

What should I track? Joint pain (0–10), morning stiffness time, sleep quality, and how far you can walk or how long you can type or stand. Patterns beat one-off ratings.

Safety and when to get urgent help

This page is general information for people in the United Kingdom, not personal medical advice. Seek urgent help via NHS 111 or A&E if you have sudden inability to move a joint, hot swollen joint with fever, chest pain, severe shortness of breath, or symptoms that feel immediately dangerous.
